clips.caption:
Say a restaurant's food wasn't very good, and by one government definition, you just published misinformation.

That's not hyperbole - Kevin walks through it literally: an opinion gets reclassified as a lie the moment a fact-checker disagrees with it. McDonald's serves great food, they rule, and anyone who says otherwise is spreading misinformation. Stretch that same definition over anything you believe, and misinformation stops meaning false. It starts meaning disagreement.

That's the actual definition being used right now.

clips.send: Sends it to the friend convinced a depopulation genocide is coming - relief, then unease at the quieter real plan underneath.
clips.caption:
You've heard an elite somewhere say we need to eliminate a billion useless eaters, and you've heard it read as a plan for mass death.

Kevin says that's not what it means, and he was in the room when it was explained: a useless eater is just someone who isn't earning and isn't spending. The actual plan isn't to kill that person off - it's to raise them out of poverty until they're earning enough to become a consumer. Elimination means economic conversion, not extermination.

Which also means the decades-old depopulation warning was never about bodies. It was about spreadsheets.

clips.send: Sends it to the friend who thinks a cashless society is just convenience - unease at what it actually trades away.
clips.caption:
Walk into the Atlanta airport today with nothing but cash in your pocket, and you can't buy anything. Not one register in the whole airport takes it anymore.

Kevin tells it from personal experience: walking out of federal prison with cash in hand, unable to spend a dollar of it at the airport. In Switzerland, he once withdrew $50,000 in notes and nobody blinked. Today, carrying that much cash there can get it legally confiscated.

A cashless world sounds like convenience. It's also the only way every transaction you make can be tracked, approved, or denied.
